title: Two noise models give 62 to 91 percent power to separate steady 2.6-minute timing clocks at KOI-3871.01 epochs
abstract: We test whether the Kepler timing design can separate two explanations of a known KOI-3871.01 timing wave. We compare steady harmonics at fixed and measured sampling phases using 1,123 selected catalog timings and release-25 clock data. Simulations refit early coefficients and use separate null calibration and evaluation draws. A steady 2.6-minute measured-clock wave gives 62.3 to 66.8 percent rejection under catalog Gaussian noise and 79.1 to 90.6 percent under residual block-wild noise across 12 phases. The observed statistic does not reject the tested fixed-clock family. The two sampled harmonic spaces overlap strongly but are not equal. The new result measures conditional test sensitivity; it does not identify the cause of the wave or confirm a planet. A finite null grid, chosen source subset, fixed wave, empirical noise assumptions and lack of independent observations limit the result. Code, aggregate results, a figure, input hashes and separate-scratch retrieval steps are included. External data remain outside the bundle.

display.caption: Rejection fractions for injected measured-clock waves. The band spans 12 phases; the line gives their mean. Each noise model uses a threshold from separate fixed-clock simulations over a finite amplitude and phase grid. Results condition on the source design, errors and noise assumptions.

citations.reason: We adapt input preparation and observed-fit code, then test the power of its inconclusive clock comparison.
The verified external timing subset supplies the selected lead and timing inputs. We apply the corrected time origin from the clock study.
Exposure-integrated flux fits give a separate method check on the same observations; our new result tests catalog clock discrimination sensitivity.
